Al Orsatti.note:
Al worked alongside his brothers Frank, Vic and Ernie in the Orsatti Agency. The family business represented performers and creative talent across film and radio; Al’s own clients included actress Peggy O’Neill.

He was the father of Ken, born Alfred Kendall Orsatti, who later became the Screen Actors Guild’s national executive director. Al died of a heart attack by 1949, aged 48; the agency’s subsequent leadership passed to Vic after both Al and Frank had died.
noteSources: Tom Weaver, David Schecter & Robert J. Kiss, Universal Terrors, 1951–1955 (McFarland, 2017), This Island Earth chapter

Vic Orsatti.note:
Ernie's brother: USC quarterback, agent to Judy Garland and Sonja Henie, later a producer. Formed Sabre Productions on Sept 17, 1953, planning This Island Earth as its first film (the picture was made at Universal). Producer credits: Flight to Hong Kong (assoc., 1956), Ride Out for Revenge (assoc., 1957), Domino Kid and The Hired Gun (1957), Apache Territory (1958), A Face in the Rain (exec., 1963), plus the CBS western The Texan (1958–60) with Rory Calhoun. Earliest credit: script clerk on Spring Fever (1927).

Born Victor Manuel Orsatti in Los Angeles, Nov 25, 1905; died Newport Beach, June 9, 1984; interred at Pacific View Memorial Park, Corona del Mar.

Mob-adjacent orbit: his first wife June Lang (m. 1937) later married Outfit figure Johnny Roselli; second wife Marie "The Body" McDonald reportedly had an affair with Bugsy Siegel in Las Vegas while divorcing him (1947).

Photos (link only): with RKO starlet Frances Neal at the Citizen Kane premiere, 1941 (Variety); at Victor Orsatti's spaghetti party with Al, Alice Faye and James Stewart (Getty). In July 1934, gossip columns reported Jean Harlow at the Legion prizefights with Vic Orsatti.
noteSources: https://www.glamourgirlsofthesilverscreen.com/show/213/Vic+Orsatti/index.html (citing Crivello, Fallen Angels; Strait, Queen of Ice)

Ernie Orsatti.note:
Ernest Ralph Orsatti (1902–1968) moved between the worlds that would shape the family archive: movies, baseball and talent representation. Born in Los Angeles on September 8, 1902, he was the sixth of seven children of Italian immigrants Maurizio and Maria (Manze) Orsatti, known in America as Morris and Mary.

He entered pictures as a young man and worked in Buster Keaton’s unit as a prop man, bit player and stunt double. Professional baseball followed: his major-league career with the St. Louis Cardinals ran from 1927 to 1935, with a .306 average across 701 games and World Series championships in 1931 and 1934.

After his last major-league game he joined brothers Frank, Vic and Al in the talent agency. Other ventures included an oddity shop and florist, a candy-vending-machine patent and, later, Orsatti Bail Bonds in Van Nuys.

He married singer Inez Gorman in September 1934; their sons Ernie F. and Frank H. carried the family into stunt work. They divorced in 1952. In 1960 he married Alice Joyce Ritchie and ran the bail-bond business with her until his death on September 4, 1968. He is buried at San Fernando Mission Cemetery.
noteSources: https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0331075/ (bio and trivia; the Met appearance is from IMDb trivia and not found in the Met archives search)
https://leadinglightsautographs.com/products/inez-gorman-singer-and-starlet-autograph-and-vintage-photo (dealer listing; also says she sang at the Metropolitan Opera – not found in the Met archives)

Inez Gorman.note:
Born October 31, 1912 in Massachusetts, she was a soprano trained at Philadelphia's Curtis Institute of Music, where on April 13, 1933 she gave the first performance of Ezra Rachlin's Goethe song "Gefunden" in Casimir Hall. She married Ernie Orsatti in Beverly Hills in September 1934, the year he won the World Series, and they had two sons who became the family's stunt dynasty: Ernie F. and Frank H.

Twentieth Century-Fox signed her around 1936 for glamour portraits by Gene Kornman; in January 1937 she was elected an active member of the American Guild of Musical Artists alongside Rose Bampton and John McCormack; and Hal Roach tested her for a vocalist part in Laurel and Hardy's Swiss Miss (1938).

In 1945 she sang as Nelson Eddy's guest soprano on CBS radio's The Electric Hour (March 11, April 8 and June 17). At MGM in the early 1950s she sang Calpurnia in the opera sequence of Strictly Dishonorable opposite Ezio Pinza, and played Mrs. Simpson in Singin' in the Rain.

In 1936 she sang at the Metropolitan Opera in Wagner's Die Meistersinger.

She and Ernie divorced in 1952; in 1953 she married Raymond Earl Pierson, her husband until her death in Glendale on December 6, 1986. Her son Ernie F. remembered the Christmas Eve parties at home, his father cooking for dozens of guests "from show business and the opera world." Ernie F. also remembered his father as a great athlete and a talented chef.

Ernie F. Orsatti.note:
Born Beverly Hills Feb 13, 1940; died La Quinta Sept 12, 2020.

Nicknamed ‘The Legend,’ he was the son of Cardinals player and agent Ernie Orsatti and opera singer Inez Gorman. A Foster Grant model and swimmer trained under Johnny Weissmuller, he also pursued baseball: he was scouted by the Dodgers out of high school and played outfield for Los Angeles Valley College by 1961.

He entered the film industry at sixteen and appeared as an actor in The Green Berets (1968), The Mechanic (1972) and The Towering Inferno (1974), where he played the firefighter hanging on to Steve McQueen outside the scenic glass elevator. His defining Poseidon Adventure fall has its own timeline story rather than being retold here.

Over his career he accumulated some 140 stunt credits, including three Death Wish films, Hot Shots!, Alien: Resurrection and American History X. Television work included NYPD Blue and Charmed; his son Noon later took over Charmed’s stunts. His later coordination work included 18 episodes of It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia (2006–08), Big Love and Furry Vengeance (2010). He earned his DGA card on Underground Aces (1981) and won Best Stunt Coordinator for a feature film for Death Wish 3 at the 1986 Stunt Man Awards, sharing the category with Gary McLarty.
noteSources: UPI Archives, March 23, 1986, "The categories and individual winners in the second annual Stuntman Awards" (lists Best Stunt Coordinator, Film: Gary McLarty for Beverly Hills Cop; Ernie Orsatti for Deathwish 3): https://www.upi.com/Archives/1986/03/23/The-categories-and-individual-winners-in-the-second-annual/4530511938000

Frank H. Orsatti (stuntman).note:
Frank Harry Orsatti was born in Los Angeles on February 26, 1942, and died in Sherman Oaks on December 23, 2004. The son of Ernie Orsatti and Inez Gorman, he pursued the family’s baseball tradition before building a career as a stunt performer, coordinator and second-unit director.

His work linked him to several of the era’s leading screen performers: he doubled Arnold Schwarzenegger in The Terminator, Burt Reynolds for nine years, and Bill Bixby in The Magician and as David Banner in The Incredible Hulk. On Hulk he also doubled the Hulk himself and directed episodes.

An original member of Stunts Unlimited, Frank coordinated Serpico, Lock Up and Highlander II, serving as sword master on the latter. His second-unit directing work included Sherlock Holmes Returns, Stark and Strays. The dated cards separately tell his baseball-to-freighters transition, first stunt jobs, Golden Gate Bridge jump and the association’s later tribute.

Rex Orsatti (Rex Pierson).note:
Credited on screen as Rex Pierson, Rex was the half-brother of Ernie F. and Frank H. Orsatti. His screen work spans stunt performance, fighting roles and stand-in work through the 1980s and 1990s.

His stunt credits include Beverly Hills Cop, Darkman, Necessary Roughness and U.S. Marshals. Road House and Lock Up brought him onto the same productions as his brother Frank.

Rex also appeared as a ‘Challenger’ fighting Rocky in Rocky III, brawled in Another 48 Hrs., and stood in on The Incredible Hulk. These varied roles place his own contribution alongside, rather than inside, his brothers’ career stories.

Noon Orsatti.note:
Son of Ernie F. He first stepped onto a set at six, filming The Seduction of a Nerd (released 1970), and joined the Screen Actors Guild in 1969; his career proper began on The Winds of War, the epic ABC miniseries shot 1980–81, when he was 18. Early on he also booked a run of national commercials – McDonald's, Sara Lee, Polaroid and more.

Stunt coordinator and 2nd-unit director. Won the 2024 Taurus World Stunt Award (Extraction 2); in the SAG Awards stunt-ensemble nominees for The Falcon and the Winter Soldier (2022).

Chad Stahelski recalls working for Ernie F. and Noon on NYPD Blue, The Pretender and Profiler – and that Ernie F. sent him to the Matrix audition.

Two 2022 Primetime Emmy nominations for Hawkeye (stunt coordination; stunt performance, "Echoes"). Co-coordinated The Expendables (2010) with Stahelski.

His long-running television work included taking over Charmed’s stunt coordination and second-unit direction from his father; the family-show timeline card tells that collaboration in full.

Rowbie Orsatti.note:
Born in 1991, Rowbie is Noon Orsatti’s son and a fourth-generation member of the family’s stunt tradition. His first show was Charmed (1998), followed by The Bernie Mac Show (2001); he joined the Screen Actors Guild in 2001.

His work developed into stunt performance and coordination. On Project X he doubled lead actor Thomas Mann and performed the roof jump. As a child on Cheaper by the Dozen he tested gags off camera for the young actors and appeared in the moon-bounce scene with Steve Martin.

His credits include Hawkeye, Extraction II, Thunderbolts* and Stranger Things (2025). He doubled Joe Locke on Agatha All Along and John Lee Ames on Ballard (2025), and coordinated Charlie Puth’s ‘Loser’ music video (2022). Film-specific memories and gags remain with their individual titles.

Ken Orsatti (Alfred Kendall).note:
Born Alfred Kendall Orsatti on January 31, 1932, Ken was Ernie Orsatti’s nephew. His father and two uncles ran the Orsatti Agency, according to the Los Angeles Times; Al’s family biography identifies Ken as his son. After earning a business administration degree from USC in 1956, he went to work as a production assistant at his uncle Vic’s Rorvic Productions.

He found his calling on the other side of the bargaining table. In 1960 he became a business representative for AFTRA, and in 1961 he moved to the Screen Actors Guild in the same role, as a theatrical business representative in Hollywood. He became Southwest regional director in 1966 and Hollywood executive director in 1971, also serving as assistant national executive director, until 1981.

From 1981 to 2000 he served as SAG’s national executive director and chief negotiator, the high point of a Guild career that ran nearly 40 years. Known for his easy demeanor, he believed the “whole idea of collective bargaining is to reach a deal.” Announcing his retirement to the national board in October 2000, he said: “It’s not easy to be leaving, but I’m leaving you as the strongest performers’ union in the world. I’m very proud of having been part of that achievement.” In 2001 he received the Ralph Morgan Award, the SAG Hollywood Division’s highest service honor, and the SAG Foundation established the Ken Orsatti Scholarship for Guild employees.

He died of pulmonary disease in West Hills, California, on August 31, 2010, at age 78. SAG president Ken Howard said he “will long be remembered for wholeheartedly working to protect the rights of our members.”

Frank P. Orsatti (agent).note:
Frank P. founded the Orsatti Agency in 1930 after a career described as bootlegging. Trade papers trace its beginnings to Bren, Weber & Orsatti; he subsequently bought out his partners and brought in brothers Al, Vic and Ernie. His clients included Judy Garland, and his business expanded beyond talent representation into Phonovision and theater candy advertising.

His association with MGM ranged from project development to a reputation as a fixer for Louis B. Mayer. Biographer Bosley Crowther called him one of Mayer’s closest companions and wrote that agents doing business at MGM had to split their fees with him. Allegations about supplying Mayer with alcohol and women are attributed to author Tim Adler, not presented as court findings; the dated timeline cards retain those accounts and their caveats.

Frank P. died of a heart attack at his Santa Monica beach home on May 19, 1947. His brother Jesse ‘Cheesy’ Orsatti was convicted in 1932 in the Caress kidnapping case and sent to San Quentin. This Frank P. was the agent, not his nephew Frank H. Orsatti the stuntman.

Stunts Unlimited.text: Frank H. Orsatti was one of the original members of Stunts Unlimited, the elite stunt association co-founded by Hal Needham, Ronnie Rondell and Glenn Wilder. In 2019 the group named him an honorary member.
Stunts Unlimited.flag: Founding year 1970 per Stunts Unlimited history; Frank described as an original member

From freighters to Planet of the Apes.text: After ten years working freighters with the Merchant Marines, Frank H. Orsatti returned to Los Angeles and took his first stunt job on Planet of the Apes (1968). Rosemary’s Baby and Bullitt followed the same year.

Frank H. tries the family game.text: Ernie’s son Frank was drafted by his father’s Cardinals and played 12 games for their Brunswick affiliate (Georgia-Florida League) in 1963 before an injury ended his baseball career. One account describes the injury as occurring in training. He later spent ten years in the Merchant Marine before becoming a stuntman.

Bootleggers to the studios.text: Family lore holds that the Orsatti brothers supplied Hollywood—and MGM in particular—during Prohibition. Weaver et al. describe Frank as ‘a former bootlegger.’ The family’s documented Prohibition court case is told in Morris Orsatti and the Prohibition agent; the later Mayer allegations are attributed separately in Handling all of MGM’s dirty work.
sources: Tom Weaver, David Schecter & Robert J. Kiss, Universal Terrors, 1951–1955 (McFarland, 2017)

Daredevil years.text: Before joining Buster Keaton’s lot, Ernie worked his way from gofer to stuntman: walking the wings of airplanes in flight, diving off cliffs, and taking car and boat gags. This was Hollywood’s barnstorming moment, when war-surplus Curtiss Jennys and aerial daredevils like Ormer Locklear were turning wing-walking into screen spectacle. ‘I wanted to be an actor, a director, a cameraman, anything that would identify me with motion pictures,’ he said.

Quitting school for the movies.text: "My interest, as a boy, was in motion pictures and not in baseball… In 1920, I decided to quit school and devote all my time to the picture business." He was seventeen when he left school for the studio lots of Los Angeles. In 1922 he joined Buster Keaton's studio as prop man and bit player – assistant property master on Sherlock Jr. (1924) and The Cameraman (1928), with stunt work on Our Hospitality (1923) and Sherlock Jr. At 5-foot-7 and 150 pounds he was nearly Keaton's double, and in Sherlock Jr.'s famous motorcycle run he was exactly that. Keaton told the story in 1958: actor Ford West "couldn't fall off the motorcycle so I took my assistant prop man… and put my clothes on him to be on the handlebars," while Keaton himself, dressed as West, took the fall. Ernie also played first base and caught for Keaton's ball team (1922–25), until former big-leaguer Turkey Mike Donlin told Keaton the kid could earn more playing baseball than working in pictures.

The Orsatti Talent Agency.text: After his last MLB game (Sept 28, 1935), Ernie joins the family’s Orsatti Talent Agency alongside brothers Frank, Vic and Al. Clients included Judy Garland, Sonja Henie, Betty Grable, Edward G. Robinson, Margaret O’Brien, Alice Faye, Frank Capra and George Stevens. His son called it the largest agency in Hollywood.

Morris Orsatti and the Prohibition agent.text: A federal indictment charged Morris Orsatti, the Los Angeles steamship and railroad ticket agent, with promising and paying bribes to Prohibition agent Harold H. Dolley (from June 1922) to drop or reduce cases against arrested liquor-law violators. Convicted on all 21 counts; the Ninth Circuit affirmed in Orsatti v. United States, 3 F.2d 778 (Feb 2, 1925), and the Supreme Court denied review on May 4, 1925. The case cut both ways: in 1923 Dolley, by then California's Prohibition chief, was himself accused of framing "Italian steamship agent Morris Orsatti", and was cleared. In November 1923 Morris Orsatti was sentenced to twenty years in the federal prison on McNeil Island and fined $2,100, then released on $50,000 bond pending his appeal. Weaver, Schecter and Kiss later described Morris, a bank vice-president, as having ties to organized crime and having “spent time up the river in the 1920s.” That characterization is from a single published source; the original agency entry flagged the prison term as not independently verified.
sources: Tom Weaver, David Schecter & Robert J. Kiss, Universal Terrors, 1951–1955 (McFarland, 2017), This Island Earth chapter
Morris Orsatti and the Prohibition agent.flag: Court record; identity with the patriarch is strongly implied (Los Angeles, same name) but not stated in the opinion. Weaver 'up the river' characterization is a single published source, not independently verified.

Orsatti Bail Bonds.text:
Ernie married Alice Joyce Ritchie in 1960 and ran Orsatti Bail Bonds in Van Nuys with her until his death on Sept 4, 1968. He is buried at San Fernando Mission Cemetery.

The Van Nuys City Directory for 1961–62 lists “Orsatti Ernie & Joyce” under BONDS BAIL at 14425 Sylvan, Van Nuys, with telephone ST 2-1319. The entry uses their personal names rather than the business name. Pacific Telephone’s March 1967 San Fernando Northwestern white pages, p. 564, later list “ORSATTI ERNEST” with the occupational abbreviation “bl bnds” at 14450 Sylvan, Van Nuys.

The Bugsy Siegel connection.text: A fan-history site claims that during Marie McDonald's 1947 Las Vegas divorce stay from Vic Orsatti she rode the Flamingo Hotel float for Siegel – that detail is from a non-scholarly source. Testimony before the Senate's Kefauver Committee tied agent Frank P. Orsatti to Siegel directly: Irving Sherman, who was in California from 1937 to 1940, said he became friendly with Benjamin "Bugsy" Siegel and went to the track with him, and that Frank Orsatti, of the Orsatti Bros. Theatrical Agency, introduced them.
sources: Kefauver Committee report (U.S. Senate), Aug 31, 1951, pp. 63–64

Frank P. Orsatti opens the Orsatti Agenc.text: "In 1930, their son Frank, a former bootlegger, went into the agency business and brought in his brothers Al, Victor and Ernie. The Orsatti Agency represented actors, executives, producers, directors, writers and radio talent." Trade papers record that Frank P., a former real estate operator, entered the business in 1930 as Bren, Weber & Orsatti, then bought out his partners and brought in his brothers Victor, Ernie and Al. The agency climbed the Sunset Strip as it grew: from 7608 Sunset to 9000 and 9121 Sunset in the 1930s, then 9130 Sunset Boulevard in the 1940s. Around 1950 it moved to 300 S. Beverly Drive in Beverly Hills, its home into the 1960s.

Ken Orsatti: SAG National Executive Dire.text: As national executive director from 1981 to 2000, Ken Orsatti was also SAG’s chief negotiator, brokering about 20 major contracts during a period of dramatic contract expansion and record-setting earnings for members. Facing studio negotiator Nick Counter through six TV and theatrical negotiations from 1983 to 1998, he reached a deal every time; the only strike of his tenure was the six-month commercials strike of 2000, in which John McGuire was the Guild’s chief negotiator. He led the campaigns that brought the advertising industry in the Guild’s branches, and stunt performers, into SAG, and he helped negotiate local and regional contracts that created work for thousands of members. He helped create the SAG Foundation in 1985 and later sat on its board. He was a trustee of the SAG-Producers Pension & Health Plans for more than 35 years and a vice president of the International Federation of Actors. When the SAG and AFTRA boards met jointly for the first time in 1995 and voted 128–8 for a merger plan, he called it “a tremendously important step toward merger,” adding: “Merger is essential for the future protection of performers’ and broadcasters’ rights.”

poseidon_funfacts.text: Ernie F. Orsatti is best known for his skylight fall in this film. Cast as Terry (Pamela Sue Martin's boyfriend), not as a stuntman, he was asked to do the 32-ft fall. Gene Hackman came to watch: "We've all come to watch you die." One take; it knocked him "colder than a cucumber."
